newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Minor crude draw seen in API data.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Minor crude draw seen in API data.

text.p: Tuesday evening's oil inventory report by the American Petroleum Institute (API) is expected to show a minor draw in crude stocks, the fifth consecutive weekly decline just as Iraq resumes crude exports.
"It strikes me that there may be some recovery in imports, but imports are still low and refinery runs are high," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown.
An average of trader forecasts in a Reuters survey showed a draw of 500,000 barrels in crude stocks for the week ended December 6.
Estimates ranged from a draw of three million to a build of two million barrels. The breakneck refinery run rate is expected to have remained steady at around 93.7 percent.

Much talked about gasoline imports from Europe may appear in this week's data, but a recovery in demand made estimates range from a draw of 500,000 barrels to a build of 1.5 million barrels. The average was a build of 825,000 barrels.

High output of distillate, which is comprised of heating oil and diesel, is expected to boost distillate stocks by 700,000 barrels. Estimates ranged from a draw of 1.5 million barrels to a build of one million barrels.

"Though demand may be high with the cold weather last week, output has been strong," said ED&F Man International trader Bob Yawger. Traders expect distillate output to have remained around its feverish 3.66 million barrels a day.
Meanwhile, the last four weeks of data have shown crude stocks dropping a total of 13 million barrels, leaving U.S. crude stocks 18 million barrels below the year ago level.
Part of the drop is traced to a rally in world crude prices which had closed the arbitrage for North Sea imports to the U.S. Gulf. Most crude imports have been coming from Latin America and Canada.
Traders and analysts also said refiners have been holding off crude purchases until the resumption of Iraqi crude exports is able to bring down prices.
"When Iraqi oil begins to be absorbed by the market, you may see an easing in prices, and the arb opening up," said Brown.

On Monday U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali gave final clearance for Iraqi oil sales under an oil-for-food accord which eases U.N. sanctions against Iraq and allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, in exchange for humanitarian aid.
